`ensure_ascii` on Flask's `DefaultJSONProvider` decides whether non-ASCII characters in JSON output are written as `\uXXXX` escapes or as literal Unicode characters. I answered from the precompiled repo notes and did not re-open the source.

**Where it lives**
- `src/flask/json/provider.py`, class `DefaultJSONProvider`.
- `ensure_ascii` is a class attribute that defaults to `True` (around L144-155).
- You can change it per app with `app.json.ensure_ascii = False`.
- You can also subclass `DefaultJSONProvider` with a different default. Then either set `Flask.json_provider_class` or assign `app.json = MyProvider(app)`.

**How it is applied**
- `DefaultJSONProvider.dumps()` (around L166-179) calls `kwargs.setdefault("ensure_ascii", self.ensure_ascii)`.
- It then calls the standard library's `json.dumps(obj, **kwargs)`.
- Because it uses `setdefault`, an `ensure_ascii` passed by the caller overrides the provider's setting.
- The escaping itself is done by the standard `json` module. Flask only supplies the default.

**Effect on output**
- With `ensure_ascii=True` (the default), non-ASCII characters are escaped, so a snowman `☃` becomes `"\u2603"`. The output is pure ASCII.
- With `ensure_ascii=False`, characters are emitted literally, so `☃` stays `"☃"`. The output then contains non-ASCII text, and the response needs to be encoded as UTF-8.

`test_json_as_unicode` in `tests/test_json.py` (around L48-54) checks both cases.

`Blueprint._got_registered_once` stops you from changing a blueprint after it has been registered on an app. Once it is set, any setup call raises an error instead of applying to only some registrations. I answered from the precompiled repo notes and did not re-open the source.

**Where it lives**
- The flag is a class attribute on `Blueprint` in `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py` (around L119). It starts as `False`.
- `Blueprint._check_setup_finished` (around L213-221) reads it.
- `Blueprint.register` (around L319-320) sets it to `True`. This happens on every registration, before the deferred functions run.

**How the guard works**
- Setup methods are decorated with `@setupmethod`, defined in `src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py` (around L42-49). The decorator calls `self._check_setup_finished(f_name)` before running the method.
- If the flag is `True`, `_check_setup_finished` raises an `AssertionError`. The message says the setup method "can no longer be called on the blueprint '<name>'" because it "has already been registered at least once, any changes will not be applied consistently."
- The decorated methods include `route`, `before_request`, `after_request`, `teardown_request`, `errorhandler`, `url_defaults`, `url_value_preprocessor`, `context_processor`, `record` and `register_blueprint`.

**Why it exists**
- `Blueprint.register` replays the deferred functions recorded by `record` and the route and hook decorators. It replays them onto each app it is registered with.
- A setup call made after a registration would be missed by the app that already ran the replay. Only later registrations would pick it up.
- Failing loudly keeps every registration of the same blueprint identical.

Flask has no separate "static component". Static serving is a feature of the shared `Scaffold` base class, and `Flask` and `Blueprint` each inherit it. The two classes each define their own `send_static_file` and `get_send_file_max_age`, and both read the same config value, which is what keeps caching consistent.

**Class hierarchy**
- `src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py::Scaffold` (L52) is the common base. It holds `static_folder` and `static_url_path`, and the `has_static_folder` property (L241) returns `static_folder is not None`.
- `src/flask/sansio/app.py::App(Scaffold)` (L59) is the base of `src/flask/app.py::Flask`.
- `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py::Blueprint(Scaffold)` (L119) is the base of `src/flask/blueprints.py::Blueprint(SansioBlueprint)` (L18).
- The sans-IO layer holds only configuration and routing state. The concrete classes add the code that reads files and builds a `Response`.

**Static serving on each component**
- `Flask.send_static_file` (`src/flask/app.py` L308) raises `RuntimeError` if no static folder is set. It computes `max_age = self.get_send_file_max_age(filename)` and calls `send_from_directory`.
- `Blueprint.send_static_file` (`src/flask/blueprints.py` L82) does the same with `self.static_folder`. It raises `RuntimeError` if `has_static_folder` is false.
- Both methods carry a comment (`app.py` L323, `blueprints.py` L97) explaining why they compute `max_age` themselves. `send_file` only knows to call `get_send_file_max_age` on the app, so each component passes its own value in explicitly.

**Consistent caching**
- `Flask.get_send_file_max_age` (`app.py` L281) and `Blueprint.get_send_file_max_age` (`blueprints.py` L55) both read `current_app.config["SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT"]`. The blueprint version uses `current_app`, not the blueprint itself.
- Both apply the same conversion: `None` stays `None`, a `timedelta` becomes `int(total_seconds())`, and any other value is returned as is. The `filename` argument is ignored in both.
- A blueprint's static files therefore get the same cache lifetime as the app's, unless a subclass overrides the method.
- `helpers._prepare_send_file_kwargs` (`src/flask/helpers.py` L387-389) is a separate path. It sets `max_age = current_app.get_send_file_max_age` for `send_file` and `send_from_directory` when the caller doesn't pass one. Those helpers use the app's method, and the two `send_static_file` methods compute their own value and pass it in.

**Route registration**
- I didn't trace where the `/static/<path:filename>` rule is added. That happens when the app or blueprint is set up or registered, not in the methods above.

`UnexpectedUnicodeError` is defined in `src/flask/debughelpers.py` (L17-20), and the dual inheritance there doesn't separate validation failures from encoding issues. It does the opposite: the class is both at once, so it can be caught as either kind of error. Nothing in the repo raises it, so it doesn't reflect a wider layered design.

**What the class is**
- It is `class UnexpectedUnicodeError(AssertionError, UnicodeError)` with only a docstring: "Raised in places where we want some better error reporting for unexpected unicode or binary data."
- A search of the repo, excluding `.micode/`, finds no other reference to it. No code in the repo raises or catches it, and nothing exports it. It looks like a leftover from older Flask, where request data was decoded as text. I can't confirm that history from the source alone.

**What the two bases signal**
- `UnicodeError` is the domain category: the problem is text encoding or decoding. Code that does `except UnicodeError` would still catch it.
- `AssertionError` marks it as a debug diagnostic, not a normal runtime error. Every exception in this module subclasses `AssertionError`. That includes `DebugFilesKeyError(KeyError, AssertionError)` at L23 and `FormDataRoutingRedirect(AssertionError)` at L50. They are "this only happens in debug mode" errors.
- `DebugFilesKeyError` uses the same combination. It stays a `KeyError`, so existing handlers still work. It also carries a better message: its `__str__` returns `self.msg` instead of `KeyError`'s repr-quoted text.

**Design consequences**
- The exception can be handled by its domain type or by its debug-marker type. Flask adds diagnostics without changing what existing handlers catch.
- `debughelpers.py` is a leaf module with debug-only helpers. It is imported lazily from debug paths in `app.py`, `wrappers.py` and `templating.py`.
- `Request._load_form_data` in `src/flask/wrappers.py` calls `attach_enctype_error_multidict` only when the app is in debug mode. That function swaps the class on the `request.files` instance, so production behaviour is untouched.
- There is no separate validation layer versus encoding layer here. The classes only mix a debug marker with the standard exception that describes the fault.

The question doesn't name a test, and two tests in the repo fit it. The closest match is `test_subdomain` in `tests/test_testing.py` (L302-318). The other candidate is `test_proper_test_request_context` in `tests/test_reqctx.py` (L63-104). I read both tests, but I didn't re-read the Flask source they exercise, so the source-side steps come from the compiled notes.

**`tests/test_testing.py::test_subdomain`**

Each step depends on the one before it:

1. **Construction.** `flask.Flask(__name__, subdomain_matching=True)` turns on subdomain matching. Without it, Flask would not match on the host's subdomain part.
2. **Configuration.** `app.config["SERVER_NAME"] = "example.com"` gives the app a root domain. That is the base for building and matching subdomain hosts.
3. **Client.** `app.test_client()` is created before the routes exist, but it is only used at the end.
4. **Route registration.**
   - `@app.route("/", subdomain="<company_id>")` goes through `Scaffold.route`, which calls `App.add_url_rule`.
   - That adds a werkzeug `Rule` with the subdomain to `app.url_map` and stores the view in `app.view_functions`.
   - It depends on step 1 because the rule is only matched by subdomain when matching is on, and on step 2 because the rule is resolved against `SERVER_NAME`.
5. **Request context creation.** `app.test_request_context()` builds an environ from `SERVER_NAME` through `flask.testing.EnvironBuilder` and pushes a request context. `url_for` needs that context.
6. **URL building.** `flask.url_for("view", company_id="xxx")` looks up the rule in `url_map` and fills in the subdomain. The result is a full URL, `xxx.example.com`. It depends on steps 4 and 5.
7. **Dispatch.** `client.get(url)` sends that URL through the WSGI stack. The subdomain is matched against the rule, `company_id="xxx"` is passed to `view`, and the test asserts status 200 and body `b"xxx"`.

The full chain is: `subdomain_matching` and `SERVER_NAME`, then `add_url_rule` into `url_map`, then `test_request_context`, then `url_for`, then `client.get`.

**`tests/test_reqctx.py::test_proper_test_request_context`**

- It sets `SERVER_NAME="localhost.localdomain:5000"` and registers `@app.route("/")` and `@app.route("/", subdomain="foo")`.
- Inside `app.test_request_context("/")`, `url_for("sub", _external=True)` must equal `"http://foo.localhost.localdomain:5000/"`.
- The rest of the test only checks that requests are accepted when `SERVER_NAME` and the environ overrides differ or match.
- It skips the client dispatch step, so it covers only configuration, registration, context creation and URL building.

**A similar test outside these two**

`tests/test_basic.py::test_subdomain_basic_support` (L1754) skips `url_for` and requests each host directly with `client.get("/", "http://test.localhost.localdomain/")`.

Blueprint template filters, tests and globals are copied into the app's one shared Jinja environment when the blueprint is registered. `render_template` later renders through that same environment, so the functions are found at render time. I checked the registration code with a grep. The rendering and context-processor parts come from the compiled notes, and I didn't re-read them.

**1. One shared environment**
- `App.jinja_env` (`src/flask/sansio/app.py` L469-477) is a `cached_property`. It calls `create_jinja_environment()` on the first access and returns the same object every time after that.
- Every template lookup and render on the app goes through this one object.

**2. Registration adds the functions to that environment**
- Blueprint methods `app_template_filter`, `app_template_test` and `app_template_global` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py` L444-551) are decorators. They call `add_app_template_filter`, `add_app_template_test` or `add_app_template_global`.
- Each `add_app_template_*` method defines a `register_template(state)` closure. The closure writes `state.app.jinja_env.filters[name or f.__name__] = f`, or the `.tests` or `.globals` equivalent (L473, L511, L549).
- The closure is queued with `Blueprint.record_once` (L233), so it does not run when the decorator is applied.
- `Blueprint.register` replays the queued closures when the blueprint is registered on an app. `record_once` makes a closure run only on the first registration of that blueprint on a given app.
- Because `state.app` is the actual app, the function lands in the same environment that renders later. The test at `tests/test_blueprints.py` L675-693 shows the global missing before registration and present in `jinja_env.globals` afterwards.
- The app-level counterparts write straight into the same dicts: `App.add_template_filter` (`sansio/app.py` L695), `add_template_test` (L738) and `add_template_global` (L776).

**3. Rendering uses the same environment**
- `render_template` in `src/flask/templating.py` gets the app from `current_app` and calls `app.jinja_env.get_or_select_template(...)`.
- Filters, tests and globals are looked up on that environment, so the blueprint's registered functions are visible.

**4. Context processors work differently**
- Context processors are not added to the Jinja environment. They are stored in the app's `template_context_processors` registry, keyed by blueprint name or `None` for app-wide ones. `Blueprint.app_context_processor` puts its function under `None`.
- `Flask.update_template_context` (`src/flask/app.py` L506) runs from the `_render` helper in `templating.py`. It merges the app-wide processors with those of the current request's blueprint, so blueprint-local processors only apply on that blueprint's requests. `tests/test_blueprints.py` L634-672 covers both kinds.

**Timing**
- A blueprint's `app_template_*` functions only take effect after `app.register_blueprint(bp)`.
- The `jinja_env` is created once and cached, so changes to `jinja_options` made after its first access have no effect.

`FakePath.__fspath__` returns `self.path`, which is whatever value was passed to the constructor. `os.fspath()` hands that value back unchanged.

**The class**
- `FakePath` is defined in `tests/test_helpers.py` (L11-22). Its docstring says it represents a `pathlib.Path` object, referring to PEP 519.
- `FakePath.__init__(self, path)` (L18-19) stores the argument as `self.path`.
- `FakePath.__fspath__(self)` (L21-22) is `return self.path`. This method is what makes the class an `os.PathLike`.

**What `os.fspath()` gets back**
- `os.fspath(FakePath("index.html"))` calls `__fspath__()` and returns the stored string, `"index.html"`.
- `__fspath__` does no conversion. `os.fspath()` accepts a `str` or `bytes` result and would raise `TypeError` for any other type. The tests only ever pass a `str`.

**Where it is used**
- The only use is `TestSendfile.test_static_file` in `tests/test_helpers.py`, at L71 in the grep output: `app.send_static_file(FakePath("index.html"))`.
- It checks that `send_static_file` accepts a path-like object and still applies the configured `SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT` cache lifetime of 3600.

The parametrization and the exception handling are two halves of one contract. `test_locate_app_raises` in `tests/test_cli.py` (L199-219) feeds `locate_app` eight `(iname, aname)` pairs. Each pair triggers a different failure path, and every path ends in `NoAppException`. The source is `src/flask/cli.py`. I did not run the tests, but I read the test and the source.

**The test**
- It is parametrized on `"iname,aname"` and does `with pytest.raises(NoAppException): locate_app(iname, aname)`.
- `iname` is the import name (`module_name`) and `aname` is the app name (`app_name`). Because they are parametrized together, each case reaches a different branch of `locate_app` and its helpers.
- Every case expects the same exception type, whichever branch fails.

**Which case hits which branch**

| `(iname, aname)` | Branch | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `("notanapp.py", None)` | `locate_app` (`cli.py` L241-264): `__import__` raises `ImportError` with no deeper traceback and `raise_if_not_found=True` | `NoAppException("Could not import ...")` (L255) |
| `("cliapp/app", None)` | Same branch; the name with a slash is not importable | same |
| `("cliapp.message.txt", None)` | Same branch; the import fails at the top level | same |
| `("cliapp.importerrorapp", None)` | `ImportError` raised inside the module, so `tb_next` is set | `NoAppException("While importing ... an ImportError was raised")` (L249-253) |
| `("cliapp.app", "notanapp")` | `find_app_by_string`: `getattr(module, name)` raises `AttributeError` | `NoAppException("Failed to find attribute ...")` (L167-172) |
| `("cliapp.factory", "create_app(")` | `find_app_by_string`: `ast.parse` raises `SyntaxError` | `NoAppException("Failed to parse ...")` (L128-133) |
| `("cliapp.factory", 'create_app2("foo")')` | `find_app_by_string` calls the factory, which raises `TypeError` because the arguments don't match | `_called_with_wrong_args` returns `True`, so `NoAppException` (L183-187) |
| `("cliapp.factory", "no_app")` | `find_app_by_string`: the attribute isn't a `Flask` instance | `NoAppException("A valid Flask application was not obtained ...")` (L194-197) |

**Why the failure is consistent**
- `locate_app` picks the lookup by `app_name`. With `None` it calls `find_best_app`, and otherwise it calls `find_app_by_string`.
- `test_locate_app_raises` only exercises `find_app_by_string`, which handles all the string cases. The `find_best_app` failure paths are not covered by this test.
- Each parse, lookup and call failure in those functions is caught and re-raised as `NoAppException`, so callers handle one type.
- The `TypeError` handling in `find_best_app` (L76-85) and `find_app_by_string` (L179-187) relies on `_called_with_wrong_args` (L94-117). It walks the traceback and compares each frame's `f_code` with `f.__code__`.
  - If a frame matches, the factory was entered and the `TypeError` came from inside it, so it returns `False` and the error is re-raised unchanged.
  - If no frame matches, the call itself failed on arguments, so it returns `True` and `NoAppException` is raised. The `create_app2("foo")` case is this one.

**Import errors**
- `locate_app` treats a missing module differently from an error inside an existing module. `sys.exc_info()[2].tb_next` is set only when the `ImportError` was raised inside the imported module. In that case `NoAppException` is raised even with `raise_if_not_found=False`.
- `test_locate_app_suppress_raise` (L222-228) checks this: `notanapp.py` returns `None`, while `cliapp.importerrorapp` still raises.
